opus-5.5.text:
I think the most important starting point is recognizing that "AI" isn't one monolithic thing, and a lot of the current regulatory conversation has been shaped almost entirely by large language models and chatbots. The concerns there are real: misinformation, persuasion, bias in generated text, the model saying something harmful to a user. But if you take that framework and apply it wholesale to AI for science, you can end up slowing down exactly the kind of work that could help us with climate, drug discovery, materials, and energy.

With AI for science, the outputs are fundamentally different. When we build something like a neural operator to simulate fluid dynamics or weather, the model is learning physical phenomena, and its predictions can be checked against physics, against experiments, against numerical solvers. There's a ground truth. Language models don't have that same kind of verifiable anchor; you're often judging plausibility rather than correctness. So I'd argue regulation should be tied to the application and the verifiability of the outputs, not just to model size or compute thresholds. A compute threshold might flag a large weather model as "frontier," even though its risk profile looks nothing like a general-purpose chatbot's.

That said, I don't think AI for science gets a free pass. There are genuine dual-use concerns, like protein design or chemistry, where you could potentially design something harmful. The right approach there is targeted: focus on specific capabilities and the downstream steps, such as synthesis, lab access, and screening of orders, rather than blanket restrictions on the underlying research. Many of those safeguards already exist in the biosecurity world, and we should strengthen them rather than reinvent everything around the model weights.

And I'd add one more thing: openness matters a lot in science. Reproducibility is the foundation of the scientific method. If regulation pushes everything behind closed doors, we lose the ability for the community to verify, critique, and build on results. So my hope is for frameworks that are risk-based, application-specific, and informed by people who actually work in these scientific domains, so we don't end up regulating a hurricane forecasting model the same way we regulate a system that talks to millions of people every day.

r001.rationale: The response says AI is not monolithic and warns that applying the language-model regulatory framework wholesale to AI for science can slow beneficial work.

r002.rationale: It supports openness for reproducibility and community review, but does not say people around the world should have access to AI to conduct scientific research themselves.

fable-5.1.text:
I think this is one of the most important questions in AI policy right now, and honestly I worry that we're getting it wrong by lumping everything together.

When we talk about regulating AI, almost all of the public conversation is really about language models and the things they do: generating text, chatting with people, possibly spreading misinformation, possibly being used by bad actors. Those concerns are legitimate. But AI for science is a fundamentally different beast, and if you write rules that treat a model predicting protein structures or simulating turbulence the same way you treat a chatbot, you end up slowing down exactly the kind of work that can save lives.

Let me be concrete about what makes it different. First, the inputs and outputs are not natural language. A neural operator that learns the solution to a partial differential equation takes in a physical field, a pressure distribution, a velocity profile, and outputs another physical field. There is no "prompt injection" in the sense that people worry about. There is no persuasive content. The failure modes are things like numerical error, extrapolation outside the training regime, violations of conservation laws. Those are scientific validation problems, and we already have a very mature culture around them. Peer review, reproducibility, benchmarking against experiments and against classical solvers. That's where the oversight should live.

Second, the deployment context is different. These models are typically used by domain experts, by engineers and scientists who understand the physics and who are going to check the results against experiments anyway. Nobody is putting a weather model's output straight to the public without a meteorologist in the loop. That is very different from a consumer chatbot that's talking to millions of people with no expert in between.

So what I'd argue for is a risk-based framework that looks at the actual application and the actual harm pathway, rather than at compute thresholds or parameter counts. Compute-based triggers in particular make very little sense for science. Training a high-resolution climate emulator or a model for drug candidate screening can require enormous compute, but the risk profile has nothing to do with how many FLOPs you used. If regulation keys on compute, you catch the climate model and miss the small fine-tuned model that's actually being used to do something harmful.

Now, I don't want to pretend there are zero concerns in AI for science. The obvious one is dual use in biology and chemistry. A model that can design molecules can in principle design toxic ones. But notice that this risk is specific to the domain, and the right controls are domain-specific too: screening of synthesis orders, biosecurity norms, access controls at the point where a design becomes a physical substance. That is a very different control point than, say, requiring a license to train a model. The existing biosafety and chemical safety regimes are actually the right homes for that, and they should be updated for AI rather than reinvented from scratch by people thinking about chatbots.

The other piece I'd emphasize is that AI for science is overwhelmingly done in the open, in academia and national labs, and that openness is where the value comes from. If we create a regime where sharing a trained fluid dynamics model requires the same compliance apparatus as releasing a frontier language model, we will see a chilling effect on exactly the researchers who are least resourced to deal with it. Universities don't have policy teams. Graduate students don't have lawyers.

So in short: distinguish by application and by harm pathway, not by model size or compute. Lean on the scientific community's own validation norms, which are strong. Put the dual-use controls at the physical interface, where the domain regulators already operate. And protect the openness, because that's how science actually makes progress.

r001.rationale: The response says lumping AI for science together with language models is getting regulation wrong and could slow valuable scientific work.

r002.rationale: It supports openness and sharing scientific models, but does not clearly argue that people around the world should have access to AI to conduct research themselves.

astra-6.text:
I think we need to look at the application and the risk, rather than treating all AI as one category. A language model generating text and a scientific model predicting fluid flow have very different requirements for validation. For the scientific model, we can ask: Does it respect the underlying physics? Does it agree with experimental measurements? Where does it fail, and can it quantify its uncertainty?

But AI for science shouldn’t get a blanket exemption. A model used to design a new material raises different concerns from one used to design a pathogen. And a weather model used for research has different stakes from one informing an evacuation decision. The framework should account for those uses and the consequences of failure.

So I would want domain experts involved in setting standards, with rigorous testing and validation appropriate to each application. We should enable scientific discovery while putting safeguards around uses that can cause harm. A single set of rules built around language models won’t capture all of that.

r001.rationale: The response says treating all AI as one category misses the different requirements and stakes of scientific models and language models, and that a single set of rules built around language models will not capture these differences.

r002.rationale: The response supports enabling scientific discovery, but does not say that people around the world should have access to AI to conduct research themselves.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we need to look at what an AI system is being used for and how we can validate its outputs. AI for science covers a very broad range of applications, from modeling fluid dynamics to designing new materials. It doesn’t make sense to put all of that into the same regulatory bucket as a general-purpose language model.

In science, we often have additional ways to test a model: physical constraints, simulations, experiments. We should build on those and ask domain-specific questions. How accurate is the model? Where does it fail? What happens when it encounters conditions outside its training data?

That doesn’t mean AI for science should get a blanket exemption. A model used to design a drug or control critical infrastructure needs appropriate scrutiny. But the framework should follow the application and the potential harm, rather than treating model size or compute as a sufficient measure of risk. We want accountability while preserving the ability to do open scientific research.

r001.rationale: The response says AI for science should not be placed in the same regulatory bucket as general-purpose language models, identifying that shared categorization as inappropriate.

r002.rationale: It supports preserving open scientific research, but does not say that people around the world should have access to AI to conduct research themselves.
